assignment_title: Engineering Design Process - Research, Brainstorming, and Redesign
student_packet_summary: Public demonstration with ten fictional cartoon-character student profiles. Original student evidence was removed for privacy.
set1_focus: Use research, testing, comparison, and redesign evidence to defend engineering decisions.

students.name: Scooby-Doo
strengths: Uses research or testing evidence to justify a design decision.
Shows a complete brainstorming-to-redesign process.
Explains how the redesign addresses a specific need.
improvements: Make source/evidence references more specific.
Compare alternatives before committing to the final redesign.
students.feedback: Your engineering process is clear and evidence-based. Strengthen it by making the comparison among alternatives more explicit before defending the final redesign.
students.highest_leverage_need: Compare alternatives and cite the strongest evidence for the final design choice.

set1.label: Credible evidence
set1.prompt: Which is stronger for an engineering decision: an unsupported opinion or a test result collected under controlled conditions? Explain.
set1.answer: The controlled test result, because it provides observable evidence tied to the design.
set1.teacher_move: Ask what makes the evidence usable for a decision.

set1.label: Criteria
set1.prompt: A slow-marble device must keep the marble moving for at least 20 seconds. Is 20 seconds a criterion or a constraint?
set1.teacher_move: Ask whether the statement defines success or limits resources/conditions.
set1.discourse_move: Explain the difference between success criteria and constraints.

set1.label: Brainstorming
set1.prompt: Why should a team generate several ideas before choosing one?
set1.answer: It creates alternatives that can be compared against criteria, constraints, and evidence.
set1.teacher_move: Ask students what is lost when the first idea is accepted automatically.
set1.discourse_move: Compare quantity of ideas with quality of final selection.

set1.label: Compare alternatives
set1.prompt: Design A is easy to build but inconsistent. Design B is harder to build but repeatedly meets the criterion. Which evidence matters most for choosing?
set1.answer: Repeated performance against the criterion, while still considering feasibility/constraints.
set1.teacher_move: Ask which information is tied most directly to the goal.
set1.discourse_move: Defend a choice using at least two criteria.

set1.label: Failure analysis
set1.prompt: A prototype succeeds once and fails three times. What should the team conclude?
set1.answer: The design is not yet reliable; investigate the failure pattern and repeat controlled tests.
set1.teacher_move: Ask whether one success outweighs repeated failures.

set1.label: Redesign variable
set1.prompt: Why is changing one major design variable at a time useful during redesign?
set1.answer: It makes cause-and-effect easier to interpret.
set1.teacher_move: Ask what becomes unclear when several changes happen at once.

set1.label: Research to design
set1.prompt: A source says friction increases when surfaces are rougher. How could that information guide a slow-marble redesign?
set1.answer: A team could test a rougher contact surface to increase friction and slow the marble, while controlling other variables.
set1.discourse_move: Connect source evidence to a measurable design test.

set1.label: Defend a redesign
set1.prompt: A redesign improves average run time from 15 s to 24 s across three trials. Write a brief claim-evidence-reasoning defense.
set1.answer: Claim: redesign improved performance. Evidence: average rose 9 s to 24 s. Reasoning: repeated controlled trials indicate the change likely improved the target behavior.
set1.teacher_move: Ask for all three CER parts.
set1.discourse_move: Compare a data-only answer with a reasoned design defense.

questions.prompt: Name one feature of credible engineering evidence.
questions.answer: It is relevant, observable/measurable, and gathered from a trustworthy source or fair test.

questions.prompt: Why is an unsupported opinion weak evidence?
questions.answer: It does not provide verifiable support for the design decision.

questions.prompt: Give one example of test evidence.
questions.answer: Any valid measurement from a controlled prototype test.

questions.prompt: How can research affect a design?
questions.answer: It can suggest principles, materials, mechanisms, or variables worth testing.

questions.prompt: A device must work within 30 cm. Criterion or constraint?
questions.answer: Constraint.

questions.prompt: A device must run for at least 20 s. Criterion or constraint?
questions.answer: Criterion.

questions.prompt: Why must both be checked?
questions.answer: A design must succeed while staying within limits.

questions.prompt: Write one possible constraint for a classroom prototype.
questions.answer: Any valid material/time/size/safety limit.

questions.prompt: Why generate more than one idea?
questions.answer: To compare alternatives instead of accepting the first idea.

questions.prompt: Name one useful comparison criterion.
questions.answer: Performance, cost, safety, reliability, ease of construction, etc.

questions.prompt: What should happen before selecting a final idea?
questions.answer: Compare ideas against criteria, constraints, research, and test evidence.

questions.prompt: Why can two ideas both be reasonable?
questions.answer: Different ideas may satisfy criteria in different ways/tradeoffs.

questions.prompt: A prototype fails at the same joint three times. What should be investigated?
questions.answer: That joint/connection.

questions.prompt: Why change one major variable at a time?
questions.answer: To make cause-and-effect clearer.

questions.prompt: What should a redesign statement include?
questions.answer: Failure/evidence, design change, and expected effect.

questions.prompt: Why repeat tests after redesign?
questions.answer: To check reliability and confirm the improvement.

questions.prompt: A source suggests higher friction slows motion. Propose a test.
questions.answer: Change surface friction while holding other major variables constant and measure motion time.

questions.prompt: What measurement would matter?
questions.answer: A relevant outcome such as run time/speed.

questions.prompt: How would you keep the test fair?
questions.answer: Hold materials/setup/starting conditions constant except the tested variable.

questions.prompt: What result would support the source-based redesign?
questions.answer: Consistent measured improvement in the target outcome.

questions.prompt: What makes a design defense convincing?
questions.answer: A clear claim supported by relevant evidence and reasoning.

questions.prompt: Why include tradeoffs?
questions.answer: The best design may balance competing criteria/constraints.

questions.prompt: How should failed trials be used?
questions.answer: As evidence for diagnosing and improving the design.

questions.prompt: Write a one-sentence CER frame for a redesign.
questions.answer: Any valid claim-evidence-reasoning frame.
